title: The Waitlist Illusion: Why a Fully Booked Psychology Practice Doesn't Always Mean a Growing One
linkedin:
Ten September is World Suicide Prevention Day. Across Australia, demand for mental health support keeps rising, and psychology practices are feeling it directly through longer waitlists.

Here is the part that surprises a lot of practice owners: a longer waitlist does not automatically mean a more profitable practice.

Revenue is set by the number of billable hours a registered clinician can actually deliver in a week, and that number barely moves no matter how many new referrals come in. Intake calls, risk screening and admin time all eat into the week without generating a dollar of billed revenue.

Add Medicare's Better Access session caps into the mix. Most clients get a capped number of subsidised sessions each calendar year, resetting on 1 January rather than at EOFY, which puts a ceiling on revenue per client regardless of how long the waitlist runs.

Then there is the workforce side. Registered psychologists are in short supply across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, and losing one experienced clinician can strip ten to fifteen billable hours a week from a practice's capacity overnight. The replacement rarely arrives fully booked from day one, so the gap between how busy a practice looks and what it is actually banking can run for a full quarter or more before anyone can point to why.

The practices that manage this well stop reading waitlist length as a single health signal. They track it alongside billable utilisation as two separate numbers, so they know whether the next hire is what will actually move revenue, or just the queue.
